Executive Summary

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap out-of-bounds write in HotSpot’s AVX-512 Base64 decoder on x86-64. Calif reported it and showed pre-auth RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Nobody has reported exploitation in the wild as of November 17, 2026. CISA issued an alert that same day, urging everyone to patch now.

Your Java4Shell Response Plan

Patch to Oracle 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1, or to your vendor’s build with JDK-8393212.

If you can’t patch today, start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restart it.

You’re only exposed on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. ARM64 isn’t affected.

Tip for Qualys customers: you can apply the step 2 flag with TruRisk Eliminate, targeting only the hosts that need it and rolling it back in one click.

Oracle shipped the fixed builds on November 17, 2026. October’s builds are still vulnerable.

Distro packages built before the fix are vulnerable even when the version looks current. Ubuntu’s 17.0.21.0.3 and Oracle Linux’s 17.0.21 are two examples.

How the Java4Shell Attack Chain Works

This is a typical Java4Shell attack chain:

The attacker needs a Base64 decode value they can control. Vulnerability discoverers were able to reach this pre-authentication condition via authentication in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after login in Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. A Java client that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server is exposed too.

The attacker then sends valid decodes until the server compiler compiles the fast path, then the bad input: 64 valid characters and one =, or 128 and one = on older 17 builds.

The target must pass the gates in the source. The JVM must see avx512_vbmi and avx512bw with UseAVX=3, the intrinsic must be on, and on 17u the input must be longer than 128 characters.

The stub’s tail handling goes wrong. The next section walks through it.

On a fixed build, or with the intrinsic off, nothing happens. Otherwise, 62 or 63 bytes land past the destination array on the Java heap.

Vulnerability researchers mentioned that they groomed the heap (G1 regions, thread-local allocation buffers) to turn that write into code execution. Unsuccessful exploitation will lead to a denial-of-service condition on the endpoint.

This remote code execution chain has only been mentioned as achieved by the vulnerability researchers. Nobody has reported it in the wild yet.

Tracing Java4Shell to Its Root Cause

Based on the jdk17u source at the fix commit, HotSpot generates the stub in generate_base64_decodeBlock (it shows up as implDecode at runtime), and C2 calls it from java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0 once that method is hot. JDK-8268276 added the AVX-512 decoder in JDK 18 and JDK-8296735 backported it to 17.0.6, so 17.0.5 and older are clean.

The whole vector decoder sits inside if (VM_Version::supports_avx512_vbmi() && VM_Version::supports_avx512bw()). Without both features HotSpot only builds the scalar 4-character loop, which is fine. 17u has no AVX2 decoder; the AVX2 tables in that file are for encoding. MIME input goes straight to the scalar loop. Basic and URL input take the vector path once it’s longer than 128 characters.

The vector code decodes 64 characters a pass, and L_finalBit handles the last 1 to 63. Before the fix, a tail of 1 to 3 characters ending in = gave an output size of 0, and the padding step subtracted 1 from it. The output mask then came from bzhiq with an index of -1. bzhiq only reads the low 8 bits of the index, so -1 became 255, nothing got cleared and the mask stayed all ones. The final masked store wrote a full 64 bytes where it should have written none.

The exact trigger condition on 17u follows from the control flow. The input must be longer than 128 characters and go through the basic or URL decoder, since MIME goes to the scalar loop. Inputs of 256 characters or more run through 256-character passes, then everything runs through 64-character passes, so the tail left at L_finalBit is the length modulo 64. Every character in those passes must be valid Base64; a = or any other bad character inside a pass makes the stub exit early and hand the rest to Java. The tail must be 1 to 3 characters ending in =, and any non-padding character in it must also be valid. Put together, the bad lengths are 64k + 1 to 64k + 3 for k of 2 or more: 129 to 131, 193 to 195, 257 to 259 and so on. Legitimate padded Base64 always has a length that’s a multiple of 4, so none of these inputs is valid anyway. Unpadded values such as JWT segments can have other lengths, but they never end in =. That makes length modulo 64 plus a trailing = a tighter hunting signal than “not a multiple of 4”.

The fix, JDK-8393212, adds four lines at L_finalBit: if fewer than 4 characters remain, jump to L_bruteForce, the scalar path. The commit title is “Base64 optimization improvements”, which tells you nothing.

The fix closes the underflow and causes no other change. The new check runs before the stub computes either the input mask or the output size. With 4 or more characters left, the output size starts at (length / 4) × 3, which is at least 3. Padding takes off at most 2, so the size stays at 1 or more and bzhiq always gets a valid index. A tail made only of = fails the validity check and drops to the scalar loop. Tails of 1 to 3 characters never reach the vector code at all. I checked memory safety only. I didn’t check whether the stub decodes every odd-length tail of 4 to 63 characters correctly, and the fix doesn’t touch that logic.

No CWE is assigned yet. I’d file it as an integer underflow (CWE-191) that causes an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Windows x64 gets the same vector code; the function only differs in how it reads its arguments there. I’ve only read the 17u source. Calif’s shorter trigger on newer lines suggests a lower threshold than 128 characters there, but I haven’t confirmed it.

Confirm Exposure From Inside the Java Runtime

A JVM is exposed only when all four of these conditions are true:

It runs on an x86-64 CPU with avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2. That covers Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire, Emerald and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Skylake-SP and Cascade Lake have AVX-512 but no VBMI.

It’s OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or 18 to 27, below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack counts too, because it ships a 17-based VM.

UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics=true, which are the defaults on those CPUs.

Attacker input reaches the basic or URL decoder in java.util.Base64. Basic auth and JWT parsing do this before login.

A quiet service isn’t safe. The attacker warms up C2 with valid decodes first.

The OS doesn’t change the bug. Windows x64 gets the same generated code as Linux, though only Linux has public testing.

I wouldn’t rely on /proc/cpuinfo. It doesn’t exist outside Linux, and an empty result looks like “not affected”. Ask the JVM what it sees instead, on any OS: java -Xlog:os+cpu -version 2>&1 | grep -oE ‘avx512f|avx512bw|avx512_vbmi|bmi2’ | sort -u java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep -E ‘ (UseAVX|UseBASE64Intrinsics) ‘

All four flags, UseAVX = 3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics = true mean that runtime is exposed. Run the check with each java binary on the host, since each runtime reports its own settings.

Turn the intrinsic off with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restart the JVM. With that flag HotSpot never generates the stub, which I confirmed in the source and on a live JVM. Oracle hasn’t published it as a workaround.

Control

Impact

Trade-off

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Low

Base64 decoding falls back to plain Java and runs slower. No one has published a number

-XX:UseAVX=2

High

Also stops it, since the VBMI decoder never gets built, but it drops every AVX-512 optimization. ARM64 JVMs won’t start with it

Move to non-VBMI or ARM hosts

High

Migration work, and a reschedule back onto a VBMI node re-exposes you

Skip -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock. Upwind reports it fails unless you also pass -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions.

CISA’s alert also suggests validating Base64 at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Boundary validation helps if it rejects padded input whose length isn’t a multiple of 4 before the decoder runs. Size limits won’t: the trigger is 65 characters on newer lines, shorter than most Basic-auth and JWT values. Limiting unauthenticated access works, but it means network ACLs or a VPN in front, because the vulnerable decode happens before login.

Mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate

For Qualys customers, the Java4Shell mitigation is available now with TruRisk Eliminate on Linux and Windows hosts, linked to QIDs such as 389494. As additional QIDs are released for different operating systems, we will test them and add support. The Cloud Agent runs it on the hosts you pick. Before it changes anything, it checks that the host has an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime, so hosts that can’t hit the bug are left alone. On the hosts that can, it adds -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and keeps whatever value was already there.

The setting takes effect when each JVM restarts, so plan restarts with the application owners. Windows services pick it up after a host reboot. After the change, the agent reports every running Java process with its effective setting, worked out in the order HotSpot applies options. A JVM it can’t read shows up as unknown, so you know where to look instead of assuming it’s covered.

Rollback is one click in the console and restores the previous value. The mitigation doesn’t reach containers; set the flag in the image or pod spec for those. Treat it as a bridge to the patched builds, since Oracle hasn’t published the flag as a workaround.

Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?Java4Shell is a heap out-of-bounds write in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM on x86-64. A malformed Base64 value can make the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of an array on the Java heap. Researchers turned that into pre-authentication remote code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

Which Java versions are affected by Java4Shell?OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, and versions 18 to 27, are affected below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack is also affected because it uses a 17-based VM. Oracle released the fixed builds on November 17, 2026: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1 and 8u513-perf. Vendor builds that include fix JDK-8393212 are also safe. Java 8 standard and Java 11 are not affected.

Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild?No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of November 17, 2026. Remote code execution has only been demonstrated by researchers. CISA issued an alert the same day urging organizations to patch now.

How do I know if my Java runtime is exposed to Java4Shell?A Java runtime is exposed only when all four conditions are true. It runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. It’s an affected version. UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics are on, which are the defaults on those CPUs. And attacker input reaches the Basic or URL Base64 decoder. Check by asking each Java binary what it sees, not by reading /proc/cpuinfo. ARM64 is not affected.

How can I close the Java4Shell vulnerability if I can’t patch yet?You can mitigate it by starting the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restarting it. With this flag, HotSpot never generates the vulnerable code. Oracle hasn’t published it as an official workaround, so treat it as a bridge until you can patch.

How do I mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate?Apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics with TruRisk Eliminate through the Qualys Cloud Agent. It automatically targets only Linux and Windows hosts that have an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime. It keeps existing JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS values, reports the effective setting for every running Java process and offers one-click rollback.

articles.title: Third-Party JavaScript Is Part of Your Attack Surface: Lessons from a Recent Supply-Chain Attack
articles.context: Start Trial References Newsweek, Cyber attack hits 178 major websites Qualys, How Web Malware Detection works Qualys, Web Malware Detection Qualys TotalAppSec product page
articles.full_text:
In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript. Most of those organizations never deployed bad code. The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service.

The attackers did not break into those websites. Instead, they exploited a weakness in the vendor’s platform to gain administrative control of some customer accounts, then modified the JavaScript those customers delivered through the vendor. The vendor’s CDN served the altered code to every visitor of an affected page.

Researchers who analyzed the injected code found it running on many organizations’ websites. It was built to steal payment card details typed into on-page forms, tamper with cryptocurrency transactions, and send readable cookies to attacker-controlled servers.

The lesson extends beyond one vendor: modern websites run code their owners did not write and often do not track.

The hidden risk of third-party JavaScript

Analytics, personalization, advertising, consent management, chat, and A/B testing all depend on external scripts. Each <script src> that points to another host lets that host run code in your visitors’ browsers with the same privileges as your own code. It can read and change the page, watch form input, read cookies not marked HttpOnly, and send data out.

That is why a third-party supply-chain compromise is different from an application compromise. The attack did not require any change to the affected organizations’ source code, servers, or pipelines. The malicious file was served from the vendor’s own CDN, with the vendor’s valid certificate, from a host every affected site already trusted. Code review and server-side monitoring had nothing to catch. One weakness in a shared platform reached many organizations in a single day.

What Content Security Policy can and cannot do

Content Security Policy (CSP) tells the browser which sources may load scripts and receive data. In this incident, the injected code loaded its main payload from an attacker-controlled domain, so a strong CSP could block it.

But much depends on the word strong. Most affected sites had either no CSP or one that still let the payload run. Allowlisting the vendor’s domain made no difference, because the malicious code came through that host. Protection came from a restrictive script-src that did not allow the attacker’s domain. ‘unsafe-eval’ let an inline fallback copy of the payload run, and ‘strict-dynamic’ extended trust to scripts the compromised snippet inserted. A tight connect-src limited exfiltration but could not stop wallet-address swapping inside the page.

Reducing third-party script risk: guidance for every organization

These practices apply to any organization that runs external JavaScript on its website.

Know what runs on your pages. Keep an inventory of every third-party script, the pages that load it, who owns it internally, and why it is needed. Include scripts added through tag managers.

Load less, especially on sensitive pages. Remove scripts that no longer serve a purpose, and keep analytics, marketing, and testing scripts off payment, login, and account pages unless they are essential.

Enforce a strict Content Security Policy. Allow only the script and connection sources each page needs, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’ and ‘unsafe-inline’, use nonces or hashes where you can, and enable violation reporting. Roll out changes in Report-Only mode first.

Keep payment entry out of reach. Hosted payment fields, served in an iframe from your payment provider’s domain, cannot be read by scripts running on your own page.

Protect cookies and sessions. Mark session and authentication cookies HttpOnly so injected scripts cannot read them, and set Secure and SameSite as well.

Pin or self-host what rarely changes. Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) for third-party files that change infrequently, or host them yourself. Scripts that change often, such as tag managers and testing tools, need monitoring instead.

Hold script vendors to a high standard. Ask providers how they secure customer accounts and code changes, and how quickly they notify customers of incidents. On your own accounts with them, enforce MFA or SSO and limit who can publish code.

Watch for changes. Monitor third-party scripts for new code, new network destinations, and unexpected behavior. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.

Plan your response. Know how to disable a third-party script quickly, and keep web, CDN, and CSP logs long enough to investigate an incident.

How Qualys TotalAppSec helps identify exposure

1. Assess Content Security Policy: QIDs 150206 and 150207

QID 150206 – Content-Security-Policy Not Implemented flags applications that send no CSP header, which leaves no browser-enforced limit on where scripts can load from.

QID 150207 – Content Security Policy Insecure Configuration flags weak elements: ‘unsafe-inline’, ‘unsafe-eval’, wildcard sources, a missing default-src, and missing or invalid reporting configuration. This incident showed the effect of one of these directly, when ‘unsafe-eval’ let the inline payload run.

A QID 150207 finding does not mean a given policy would have allowed this particular attack. That depends on the full policy, including script-src, trusted sources, and nonces or hashes. Treat these findings as starting points for a policy review. Reporting matters as well. The vendor’s first investigative recommendation was to review CSP violation reports, and sites without reporting had none to review.

2. Discover external JavaScript dependencies: QID 150545

QID 150545 – JavaScript Library Loaded via External Server reports out-of-scope JavaScript libraries found during crawling, including the page, library version, and external URL. It does not judge whether a library is malicious. Its value is visibility: an inventory of external scripts is the basis for deciding which vendors to trust and which hosts a CSP should allow.

3. Find applications that serve known malicious scripts 533507 (new)

We have released QID 533507 – Known Malicious Script Reference Detected. This unauthenticated check sends an HTTP GET request and inspects the response body for a script src referencing known malicious scripts.

Use it to inventory which applications load known malicious scripts and to prioritize the applications handling payments or cryptocurrency for CSP review.

Detecting malicious content with Qualys Web Malware Detection

TotalAppSec shows where you are exposed and how well your controls are configured. Qualys Web Malware Detection asks a different question: is malicious content present? Qualys Web Malware Detection combines heuristic analysis (signature rules for patterns such as encoded JavaScript); behavioral analysis (visiting the site with a vulnerable browser and watching for unexpected file writes or processes); reputation checks of pages, referenced URLs, and remotely loaded resources against public blacklists; and antivirus scanning of downloaded scripts and files. Three detections relate directly to third-party script risk:

QID 207003 – A Match to a Known Virus was Detected: a file written to disk during page rendering is identified as malicious by a virus scanner.

QID 208000 – Content was Loaded from a Remote Malicious Page: a page loads scripts, iframes, or images from a blacklisted domain.

QID 208001 – A Link to a Malicious Page was Found: a page links to a domain on one or more blacklists.

Reputation-based detection depends on a domain being blacklisted at scan time. Attacker infrastructure is often new: Report URI found this campaign’s primary domain was registered the morning the attack began. Continuous scanning, alongside preventive controls such as CSP, is paramount for that reason.

Together, these findings give three different views. A script reference (QIDs 533507, 150545) shows where you depend on someone else. A weak control (QIDs 150206, 150207) shows how much damage a compromised dependency could do. Malicious content (QIDs 207003, 208000, 208001) is evidence that something harmful is present.

Recommendations for security teams

Follow the actions in the vendor’s report. Confirm which pages ran the snippet during the exposure window, review CSP violation reports and outbound requests against the published indicators of compromise, and keep your web, CDN, and CSP logs. The vendor and Report URI published different indicators, so check both.

For every organization:

Inventory third-party scripts. Use QIDs 533507 and 150545 to see which applications load external JavaScript, and from where.

Restrict trusted sources. Remove unneeded scripts, especially from payment, login, and personal-data pages.

Implement CSP and assess it continuously. Resolve QID 150206 and 150207 findings, keep script-src and connect-src restrictive, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’, and test changes in Report-Only mode.

Monitor third-party script changes. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.

Investigate malicious content. Treat Web Malware Detection findings as triggers for investigation.

Remove unauthorized scripts and remediate. Restore known-good code and rotate secrets stored in readable cookies.

Reassess after remediation. Rescan to confirm that fixes are in place.

Conclusion

The incident here did not require breaching a single customer’s application. It required one weakness in a platform those applications trusted. Securing a web application means having visibility into both the code you write and the external scripts you allow to run in your users’ browsers. articles.title: NGINX2Root: Five nginx Flaws, Led by CVE-2026-123007. How to Find, Mitigate, and Patch Now
articles.context: We will add distribution-specific detection QIDs to this blog as they are released
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker processes, and researchers have demonstrated remote code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker. Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. This could involve chaining the NGINX vulnerability with a suitable local privilege-escalation flaw.

Unpatched builds of NGINX Open Source from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and unpatched NGINX Plus builds, are in scope when HTTP/2 is enabled. Fixes shipped in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and turning off HTTP/2 closes this exposure where patching has to wait. A separate Linux kernel flaw that the researchers used to go from the worker account to root has no patch yet. Start with internet-facing nginx servers that accept HTTP/2, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Flaw in nginx Could Hand Attackers the Front Door to Your Applications. nginx is often the first system a web request reaches. It runs as a web server, a reverse proxy (a server that passes requests to the applications behind it), a load balancer, and the entry point to Kubernetes clusters. CVE-2026-123007 is in nginx’s own HTTP/2 code, so no application behind it has to be at fault.

HTTP/2 lets a client tell the server how much data it is allowed to send. nginx can lose count of that allowance when a client cancels requests at the right moment. The bad count later makes nginx copy memory it should not touch.

F5 says the result is typically a crash of the nginx worker, the process that handles live traffic. F5 also says code execution is possible where ASLR, the memory-address randomization that makes exploits harder, is disabled or bypassed. Xint, the team that named NGINX2Root, reports doing exactly that: it leaked memory addresses and then ran commands as the nginx worker over a public HTTPS port.

In Qualys TRU’s assessment, three outcomes matter to the business:

Exposure of traffic and keys. Code running in the worker can read requests and responses after nginx decrypts them, including passwords and session tokens. It may also expose TLS private keys that are held in software and accessible to the worker.

A foothold behind the perimeter. Backend systems usually trust the proxy in front of them. An attacker on that proxy starts from a trusted position.

Outages. A failed attempt can still crash workers and drop connections.

Workers normally run under a restricted account. An attacker gets whatever privileges the worker actually has, so if it already runs as root, no further escalation is needed in that environment. Where it does not, the researchers chained a separate flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code to get root. SCTP is a network protocol, like TCP, that the kernel supports. They report root on the host, including from nginx running inside a Docker container. That kernel flaw has no CVE and no patch yet, so patching nginx removes the remote entry point but not the step to root.

NGINX2Root covers four more nginx flaws. F5 scores all five 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1, and the same nginx releases fix them. Each needs a different configuration:

The rest of this post focuses on CVE-2026-123007, the flaw with the widest reach.

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, the attacker must also be able to open an HTTP/2 connection to nginx itself.

F5 notes that it did not evaluate versions past End of Technical Support. F5 also lists BIG-IP, BIG-IQ, and F5OS as not vulnerable in its advisory.

The checks below come from the researchers’ write-up. Run them on the nginx host. The first shows whether the build includes HTTP/2. The second shows whether the configuration turns it on.

Run this one from outside your network. ALPN protocol: h2 means the server accepts HTTP/2 from the internet.

openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E ‘ALPN protocol:|No ALPN negotiated’

nginx also ships inside other software. Status as of November 18, 2026:

Three cautions when scoping:

Do not rely on nginx -v alone. Distributions often fix a flaw without changing the nginx version number. Compare the full package version with the distribution’s advisory.

Check where the HTTP/2 connection ends. If a CDN or load balancer handles HTTP/2 in front of nginx, an outside test only reaches that device. Test the nginx port directly.

Use internet exposure to order the work, not to close findings. An internal nginx with HTTP/2 on is still reachable by an attacker who is already inside the network.

Exploitation Status

As of November 18, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild.

Working exploit code is public. The team behind NGINX2Root also reports its own exploit working over public IP addresses on AWS, GCP, and Azure, and is holding back the final steps.

The public exploit is hard to use. It sends a very large number of HTTP/2 control messages over one long-lived connection for several minutes, has to reach nginx directly, and depends on a specific memory-copy routine in the standard Linux C library on 64-bit Intel and AMD processors.

These limits slow mass exploitation. In Qualys TRU’s assessment, they do not protect a specific internet-facing server from a capable attacker, and other techniques may follow.

What to Do Now

Updating nginx is the only complete fix. F5 released fixed builds on November 18, 2026.

FIXED BUILD

1.31.9

1.30.7

NGINX OPEN SOURCE, OLDER BRANCHES

1.9.5 through 1.29.x

None listed. Move to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or use a vendor package that contains the fix

NGINX PLUS 37.1 AND LATER

Linux distributions publish on their own schedules. As of November 18, 2026, Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed package and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-123007.

Restart nginx after you update. A reload applies configuration changes but keeps the old program running, so the flaw stays in memory until a restart.

If you cannot patch today, turn off HTTP/2 on every affected listener. F5 states the flaw affects only configurations that use HTTP/2, and the researchers recommend this as a temporary measure. For the exact steps, see nginx’s documentation for the http2 directive, CERT-EU’s advisory, and section 3.3 of the researchers’ write-up. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1. Services that need HTTP/2, such as gRPC, will stop working, so test first. This covers CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 only, and it does not replace the patch.

Advice for Risk and Vulnerability Management Teams

Qualys TRU’s advice for the teams running this response:

Do not let the score set the deadline: Under CVSS v3.1 this flaw is 8.1, which many remediation policies file as High. Public exploit code and a server that faces the internet matter more than the number. Handle vulnerable nginx deployments with externally reachable HTTP/2 as an emergency.

Close findings on evidence: A server is done when the fixed build is installed, nginx has been restarted, and the vendor’s advisory confirms the package covers all five CVEs. Report patched, temporarily mitigated, not exposed by configuration, and unknown as separate states, and do not count unknown as safe.

Fix the template as well as the server: Update container images, Helm charts, machine images, and autoscaling templates. Otherwise the next scale-out or failover brings the vulnerable build back.

Put an end date on every workaround: Turning off HTTP/2 covers two of the five flaws, and the next configuration push can undo it. Record who owns each exception and when it ends.

Decide what to do with nginx that will not get a fix: The community ingress-nginx project is archived, and the older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, although fixed NGINX Plus 37.x releases exist. These need a migration plan or a signed risk acceptance.

Treat privilege escalation flaws as part of this response: Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. The newly disclosed SCTP flaw is one such path, and any other local privilege-escalation flaw that can be exploited from the worker’s context could serve the same purpose. Patch known local privilege-escalation flaws on nginx hosts, in the kernel and elsewhere, with the same urgency. A current kernel does not mean the SCTP flaw is fixed, because that flaw has no patch yet.

Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) lists every asset with nginx installed, along with the version of each installation, so teams can quickly scope NGINX2Root remediation. Because NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is affected, the version tells you which installations are in range. It does not tell you whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a Linux distribution has backported the fix, so check those separately. nginx bundled in containers, Kubernetes ingress controllers, and appliances may not appear in a standard inventory, so check those separately too.

articles.title: Why AI-ROC Is the Future of Exposure Management
articles.context: The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that vulnerability exploitation was the leading way attackers got in, while the median time to patch grew to 43 days
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Security teams have never had better visibility into their assets, vulnerabilities, and threats. What they lack is the speed to act on it. Frontier AI models are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than ever, attackers are using the same models to exploit them within hours, and most remediation still depends on scans, tickets, and change windows. Exposure management needs a new operating model that detects exposures as soon as they are disclosed, focuses only on what is proven exploitable, and remediates autonomously without breaking the business. That operating model is the AI-native Risk Operations Center (AI-ROC).

On October 13, 2026, Microsoft released the largest Patch Tuesday in its history, fixing 1,414 vulnerabilities. That is more than seven times the 193 vulnerabilities Microsoft fixed in October 2025. One of the new vulnerabilities was already being exploited, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) set a deadline of just three days to patch it.

At ROCon Americas 2026, we made the case that most organizations are focused on the wrong question. Knowing how many exposures you have is no longer useful on its own. What matters is how quickly you can turn those exposures into verified risk reduction.

The Vulnerability Surge Has Outpaced Remediation

Over the last twenty years, the security industry has gotten very good at finding things. Organizations now have more data on assets, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, threat intelligence, and alerts than ever before. The ability to fix what matters has not kept up.

Frontier AI has made that gap much wider. These models are not creating new vulnerabilities. They are surfacing flaws that already existed in code, and they are doing it much faster than before. The last two Patch Tuesdays, with 974 vulnerabilities in September and more than 1,400 in October, show how fast this is moving. Attackers have access to the same AI tools and are using them to weaponize new vulnerabilities within hours. In September, two of the vulnerabilities Microsoft disclosed were already being exploited before a patch was available.

The way most organizations remediate has barely changed. A scanner detects the vulnerability, a second tool adds asset context, a third ranks it, an attack simulation tool tests it, and a ticket is created in the hope that someone fixes it within a 30- or 60-day service-level agreement (SLA). Each of those handoffs adds time, and risk only goes down when the fix is actually applied. This process was not built for attackers who move in hours.

What the Surge Means for Security Teams

Remediation timelines are shrinking from weeks to days, but the resources to meet them are not keeping pace.

SLAs are moving from weeks to days. The 30- and 60-day SLAs most programs were built around no longer match the threat. Critical vulnerabilities now need to be patched in days, and mandates from CISA and CERT-In, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, can require remediation in as little as 12 to 24 hours.

Exploitation is how most breaches now start. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that vulnerability exploitation was the leading way attackers got in, while the median time to patch grew to 43 days.

Budgets and headcount are not keeping pace. Only 15% of security leaders expect their budgets to grow by more than 10%. Hiring more analysts is not a realistic answer.

There are too many findings to fix. One large Qualys customer had 62.5 million findings. No team has the time or budget to work through that many.

The Ideal Operating Model for Exposure Management

None of this is a new problem. Exposure management still comes down to the same basics of visibility, prioritization, and remediation. What has changed is the speed at which each of them has to happen.

Detection must happen in real time. New exposures should be identified as soon as a vulnerability is disclosed, not after the next scheduled scan.

Prioritization must be based on proof. Risk scores tell you what could be dangerous. Teams need to know whether an attacker can actually reach and exploit the vulnerability in their environment.

Remediation must take hours, not a month. Low-risk fixes should be automated, and every fix should be checked to confirm it worked.

These steps also need to run on one platform. Every handoff between separate tools and teams adds delay, and that delay is the window attackers use.

Qualys calls this operating model the Risk Operations Center (ROC). When AI agents handle the time-sensitive work at each stage, it becomes an AI-native ROC, or AI-ROC.

How Qualys Operationalizes the AI-ROC

The Qualys AI-ROC brings this operating model together on the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management Platform. It pulls in every asset and exposure across cloud, on-premises, operational technology (OT), Internet of Things (IoT), mobile, and AI environments, enriches them with threat intelligence and business context, and then prioritizes and remediates the risk that matters. Three AI agents handle the work that has to happen at machine speed: Agent Insta for detection, Agent Val for validation, and Agent Sara for remediation.

AI-Speed Detection with InstaScan

With traditional scanning, a vendor has to write a detection signature, roll it out, and then customers have to rescan their environment. That can take a day or two before a team even knows it is affected. InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta, monitors vendor advisories around the clock and matches them against the asset and software data customers already have. No new scan is needed. After the October release, Agent Insta customers had detections within five minutes.

Hyper-Prioritization with TruConfirm

Even after applying threat intelligence and business context, a large organization can still be left with hundreds of thousands of findings. TruConfirm, powered by Agent Val, tests whether those findings can actually be exploited in the customer’s environment, using production-safe payloads that never download malware. For the customer mentioned above, this reduced 62.5 million findings to 60,000 that were confirmed exploitable.

Zero-Day Remediation with TruRisk Eliminate

Detection and prioritization only matter if the risk gets fixed. Before launching TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence, we kept asking why teams were not remediating faster. Automation was not the blocker, since patch automation tools have existed for years. Confidence was. Teams did not know whether they were choosing the right fix, whether a patch would crash a business application, or whether compensating controls already covered the risk.

TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence is built to answer those questions and to be the system of record and system of action for cyber risk reduction. It takes prioritized findings from Qualys or third-party tools and recommends the right fix for each one. A patch reliability score shows how likely a patch is to deploy without issues, and integrations with firewalls and other controls show when a compensating control already covers the risk. Patching is not always the answer. If a company has moved from Zoom to Microsoft Teams and a Zoom zero-day is disclosed, the right action is to uninstall Zoom rather than patch it.

Agent Sara plans the rollout. Low-impact updates such as browsers and standalone utilities are patched automatically with no reboot required. Production workloads are patched in rings, starting in a lab environment, with health monitoring through partners like Dynatrace. If CPU, memory, or network indicators show a problem, Agent Sara stops the rollout and rolls the patch back. When a patch is not safe to deploy, Agent Sara applies a mitigation instead.

Trust Is Built Into the AI-ROC

As soon as agents start remediating, security and IT teams ask the same four questions. The AI-ROC answers each one with a setting the team controls.

What breaks if the agent gets it wrong? Every patch carries an AI reliability score based on real-world deployments. Dependency and downtime impact are known before anything is approved, and rollback is staged in advance.

Can we start small and prove it? Deployment waves let teams start with zero-touch automation for low-impact fixes, use ring-based rollouts for everything else, and keep tighter control over their most critical systems. Each team decides where to start.

How do I know why it did that? ROCky, the Qualys conversational AI interface, and every agent show their reasoning, including the threat, the affected asset, any compensating control, and the TruConfirm evidence behind each action.

Can I take the wheel back? Each wave can have its own approval gate. Rollback happens automatically if a service degrades, and nothing is marked closed until it has been revalidated.

Policy, risk appetite, confidence thresholds, approval gates, and exceptions stay with the security team, and the agents work within those boundaries. Autonomy is not something teams have to take on faith. They control how much of it to use, and the program can grow with the environment instead of with headcount.

How the Three Agents Handle a Zero-Day

At ROCon, we walked through how the agents worked together on CVE-2026-81963, a Windows vulnerability from the September Patch Tuesday that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on the same day. Agent Insta detected it in the customer’s environment within minutes of disclosure. Agent Val confirmed it was exploitable on the customer’s assets. Agent Sara saw that the patch required a reboot and already had a low reliability score, so it deployed to the lab environment first. When health indicators showed issues, Agent Sara rolled the patch back and applied a temporary mitigation, reducing the risk without the patch ever reaching production.

What Comes Next for the AI-ROC

Organizations can adopt the AI-ROC in stages. The journey begins with AI-speed detection, then extends CTEM across every tool already in use, moves to autonomous risk elimination, and finally quantifies cyber risk in business terms for the chief information security officer (CISO), the chief financial officer (CFO), and the board. Each stage builds on the one before it, so teams see results early while working toward a fully autonomous program.

The AI-ROC will continue to grow with the attack surface. As applications, AI systems, and more advanced attack techniques create new kinds of exposure, they will come into the same platform, the same risk view, and the same agent-driven workflows.

Agentic ROC Studio and the Future of Agentic AI in Risk Operations

The next step is Agentic ROC Studio, a concept Qualys is building toward. Every security team has its own runbooks, its own tools, and its own way of working, and no set of prebuilt agents can cover all of it. Agentic ROC Studio is designed to let teams build agents around how they already operate. A team would describe what an agent should do in plain language, choose the tools it is allowed to use, and have it running in minutes, with no scripting required.

These agents would work alongside the Qualys AI agents for exposure, threat, patch, and compliance, and connect to third-party tools and agents across security, IT, cloud, and identity to run as one cross-domain workflow. That is where agentic AI in risk operations is headed: a digital workforce that takes on the repetitive work across the entire risk program, while the security team sets the rules and stays in the loop.

Conclusion

Frontier AI has changed the pace of vulnerability management. Record Patch Tuesdays have arrived for two consecutive months; attackers can weaponize new flaws within hours, and the SLAs most programs were built on no longer hold. Adding more scanners, more findings, and more tickets will not close that gap.

What closes it is an operating model built for AI speed. That means detecting new vulnerabilities as soon as they are disclosed, proving which ones can be exploited, and remediating them autonomously with safeguards that let teams trust the results. The AI-ROC brings all of this together on one platform, with AI agents doing the work at machine speed and security teams in control of every decision that matters.

Every tool on the market can tell you how many exposures you have. The organizations that stay ahead in the frontier AI era will be the ones that can answer a harder question: how quickly can we turn exposure into verified risk reduction?

Ready to see how the Qualys AI-ROC detects, validates, and remediates exposures at AI speed? Watch the full session from ROCon Americas 2026, then try it in your own environment with a free 30-day trial of Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM).

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

What Is an AI-ROC?

An AI-native Risk Operations Center. It detects exposures as soon as they are disclosed, proves which are exploitable, remediates with guardrails, and revalidates before closure. Security teams set policy and stay in control.

What Do the Three Agents Do?

Agent Insta handles detection. Agent Val handles validation. Agent Sara handles remediation, including reliability scoring, ring rollouts, and rollback.

Can the Agents Patch Without Approval?

Only within the boundaries the team sets. Low-impact updates can be zero-touch. Each wave can have its own approval gate. Rollback is automatic if a service degrades. Nothing is marked closed until it has been revalidated.

What Is Agentic ROC Studio?

How Fast Does InstaScan Detect?

Running zero-day response as a service, at enterprise scale, puts specific demands on the platform underneath. Cognizant needed three capabilities working as one:

One record for every asset, across every tool, built from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, so there is no reconciling data across disparate tools before anyone can act.

Exploit validation in each client’s own environment, so every hour of the client’s team’s time goes to risk that is real.

Remediation with confidence, so automation can be trusted within production systems.

Qualys delivers all three on one platform, with the agentic AI to run them at machine speed.

Cognizant brings what a platform alone cannot: Cyber Vulnerability Management services and threat intelligence, delivery experience inside large enterprises, and a view of risk in financial terms for the board. Its operators run the Risk Operations Center, powered by Qualys ETM to navigate inside each client’s own tools, change windows, and approvals. Clients keep control of what gets fixed and when. Cognizant carries the daily work.

“Our 2026 Cybersecurity Pulse Poll shows that strength in one control, such as detection or remediation, still leaves enterprises exposed in the AI era. Together with Qualys, we are connecting detection, prioritization and remediation into one managed operating model, helping clients reduce risk, strengthen resilience and scale AI with confidence.” — Vishal Salvi, SVP and Global Head of Cybersecurity, Cognizant

Cognizant will deliver four mROC services on the Qualys platform:

Cyber risk quantification and advisory services. Cyber risk for business applications shown in dollars, with a personalized risk plan and a report for the board.

Onboarding and integration. The security tools a customer already owns connected into one record for each asset, with data quality checked from day one.

Risk monitoring as a managed service. AI-speed alerts on new CVEs, a validated queue instead of noise, and a weekly exposure review, using InstaScan, Agent Val, and ROCky.

Risk remediation as a managed service. A wave-based plan built from the Risk Elimination Playbook, zero-touch remediation where it is safe, and proof the fix held, using TruRisk Eliminate, TruConfidence, and Agent Sara.

AI-Speed Detection: Every Exposure Known in Minutes

Frontier AI has changed the rhythm of disclosure. Vulnerabilities now land in volume, and attackers act on them in hours, well inside any scan cycle.

Qualys InstaScan, delivered by Agent Insta, closes that gap. It turns the inventory and telemetry a client already has, from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, into high-confidence findings within minutes of disclosure. No new scan, no new agent.

On November’s Patch Tuesday, InstaScan delivered 90% of detections within minutes. The first landed about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own release notes went live. With Cognizant, that speed turns into action. Through its risk monitoring service, Cognizant analysts watch for new disclosures every day, confirm each exposure, and route it to the right asset owner with context. The client’s team no longer chases owners or rebuilds asset lists every time a new CVE trends.

Hyper-Prioritization: Proven Exploitability

More vulnerabilities do not mean more risk. Of the 48,172 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025, the Qualys Threat Research Unit found only 357 (0.74%) confirmed remotely exploitable and actively weaponized. No team can work the full list, and none should have to.

Agent Val and TruConfirm test what is actually exploitable in the client’s own environment, with existing controls counted. Critical on paper but blocked by a control? It leaves the urgent queue. Exploitable on a PCI-scoped server? It goes to the top.

Cyber Risk Quantification (CRQ) then puts validated risk in dollars, by business application, so the CISO can show the board what each fix is worth.

With Cognizant, the short list becomes a working rhythm. Through its risk monitoring and advisory services, Cognizant keeps each client’s validated queue current and reviews it with them every week. The client’s team stops triaging noise and starts each week knowing exactly what to fix first.

Autonomous Remediation: Remediate with Confidence and Maintain Operational Resiliency

That fear is why the global mean time to remediate sits at about 30 days. TruRisk Eliminate, with TruConfidence, removes it by protecting operational resiliency before, during, and after every change.

Before: TruRisk Eliminate chooses the safest fix for each finding: patch, mitigate, isolate, or uninstall. A patch reliability score decides what deploys automatically and what goes ring by ring.

During: Changes roll out in waves, starting with low-risk rings. System health is watched through each wave, and rollback restores a known-good state if health drops.

After: AI-powered patch failure analysis pinpoints why a change failed and the corrective actions, and automated rollback restores a known-good state.

Showing clients the 1% that matters

Cognizant can open every client engagement with a Risk Elimination Playbook, powered by TruConfidence and built for that client’s environment. It narrows the backlog to the 1% that must be fixed now and moves the rest into planned software updates. It also benchmarks the client’s mean time to remediate against peers, and shows how much of the backlog autonomous remediation can close, and how much faster.

It becomes the plan behind every remediation wave and the baseline for every review.

Where Managed Security Goes Next

The three pillars together provide a new kind of service: 24-hour autonomous remediation, run from ETM. Cognizant can take a critical zero-day from disclosure to remediation within a day, for every client, with operational resiliency built in at every step.

Managed security is moving from raising alerts to closing risk. Cognizant is among the first to deliver that at enterprise scale, and I expect it to set the bar enterprises hold every provider to. That is what the Global mROC Alliance was built for: the platform, the certification path, and the operating model to run the Risk Operations Center as a service.

Attackers already move at AI speed. This expanded partnership helps tip the balance back toward the defense.

articles.context: Executive Summary Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. The researchers who found it rate it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can corrupt Java heap memory, read secrets from it, and reach remote code execution. Researchers demonstrated pre-authentication RCE on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Unpatched OpenJDK builds from 17.0.6 onward, from any vendor, are affected when they run on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Xeon from Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC from Zen 4 onward. Oracle released fixes on November 17, 2026, and a single JVM flag closes the exposure where patching has to wait. CISA has issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately. Start with internet-facing identity, CI/CD, and collaboration systems, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Critical Java Flaw Could Hand Attackers Your Identity and Build Servers.

Java4Shell is in the Java runtime itself, so no application or library has to be at fault for a service to be exposed. The flaw sits in handwritten assembly that speeds up Base64 decoding with AVX-512 instructions. A short malformed input makes that code write 62 bytes past the end of a buffer before Java rejects the input.

Base64 carries login headers, tokens, and file uploads, so the vulnerable code often runs before a user has authenticated. Calif, the firm that discovered the flaw, demonstrated remote code execution against the following products in their default configurations:

Access required

Products

None (pre-authentication)

Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederate

Authenticated user

Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker

The researchers say these lists are not exhaustive. They also reached RCE in sample applications built on Apache Struts and Spring Boot.

The pre-authentication list is where the business risk concentrates. Identity providers issue the tokens every other system trusts, and build and artifact servers sign and ship your software. A compromise of either can expose downstream systems that trust its identities, tokens, or software artifacts.

Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, attacker-controlled data must also reach the vulnerable Base64 decoding path in the application.

Condition

Affected

Not affected

Java runtime

Unpatched OpenJDK-based builds from 17.0.6 onward, including 21, 25, and 27. Also Oracle Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf

Releases before 17.0.6, including standard OpenJDK 8 and 11. Also any vendor build that contains the fix

Processor

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids), AMD EPYC and Ryzen (Zen 4 and newer)

ARM64, and x86-64 without AVX-512 VBMI

The runtime condition covers every OpenJDK-based distribution: Oracle Java SE, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, and Red Hat OpenJDK. There is one exception on Java 8. Oracle lists the 8u511b33-perf build of Java SE 8 as vulnerable.

On Linux, run this command to check the processor. The host meets the hardware condition only if all four flags appear.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’

Two cautions when scoping:

Check the runtime each application actually runs. Many products and container images bundle their own JDK, which operating system updates do not touch. CISA notes that bundled runtimes, including those in appliances, may not appear as separate entries in a software inventory.

Use the processor condition to order the work, not to close findings. A workload on an unaffected CPU today can land on an affected one after an instance resize or a move to newer hardware.

Exploitation Status

As of November 17, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild. Do not plan around that. The trigger is a short malformed Base64 string; the root cause and exploitation technique are public, and the researchers have said details of the bug leaked before the patch.

The researchers are holding back their product-specific exploits until organizations have had time to upgrade, and plan to publish them later. They report finding the bug with AI assistance in about an hour and having a first working exploit two hours after that, for under $200 in AI token costs. Expect others to repeat that work.

There is one limit worth knowing. No universal exploit exists: each product needs its own chain, and the technique is sensitive to network conditions. That slows mass exploitation. It does not protect a specific target such as your identity provider.

What to Do Now

Updating the Java runtime is the only complete fix. Oracle released fixed builds on November 17, 2026.

Oracle Java SE

Fixed build

8 Enterprise Performance Pack

8u513-perf

17

17.0.21.1

21

21.0.13.1

25

25.0.5.1

27

27.0.1.1

Other OpenJDK vendors publish on their own schedules. As of November 17, 2026, Amazon had released Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 with the fix. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed build and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-114938.

If you cannot patch today, there is a temporary workaround. It is a startup setting for Java, applied by the team that runs the application, and it takes effect after a restart. You need only one of the two options below.

Preferred: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. This turns off the fast Base64 decoder where the bug lives. Java falls back to its standard decoder, and everything else runs as before. Applications that decode large amounts of Base64 may run slower, so test first.

Alternative: -XX:UseAVX=2. This turns off a wider set of processor optimizations, including the vulnerable one, so the performance cost is broader. Use it only on Intel and AMD servers. Java on ARM does not accept this setting and will not start.

Neither option replaces the patch.

Either way, restart every Java process. A patch or a flag takes effect only when the JVM restarts, so verify the running process and not only the installed package. Do not rely on a reverse proxy as a control. Request buffering breaks some exploit chains but is not a general mitigation.

Reduce exposure while you wait for a patch. Take identity, build, and collaboration consoles off the open internet, or put them behind a VPN, until they are patched. CISA also suggests validating Base64 input and enforcing input-size limits at the application boundary. Size limits alone will not stop this bug, because the malformed input is very short. The JVM flag above is the more direct stopgap because it removes the vulnerable code.

Work in this order:

Internet-facing identity providers such as Keycloak and PingFederate.

Internet-facing Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and Artifactory.

Other internet-facing Java services that handle logins, tokens, or file uploads.

Internal Java systems, starting with Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.

Assign an owner and a remediation deadline to every system that is waiting on a vendor build.

What to Watch For

CISA advises monitoring for rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. Qualys TRU suggests starting with these checks:

Unexpected JVM crashes or restarts on internet-facing Java services.

Java processes that start a shell or open outbound connections they have not made before.

Java runtimes on a host that your inventory does not account for.

How Qualys Can Help

Qualys helps you respond to Java4Shell: discover and assess exposure using Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM). It inventories Java installations across your assets and helps put internet-facing ones first.

Use the following CSAM query to identify potentially affected OpenJDK installations across Java 17, 21, 25, and 27 for further assessment.

As distributions publish their own advisories, InstaScan turns them into findings without waiting for the next scheduled scan.

Qualys is releasing the following detection QIDs. We will add distribution-specific detection QIDs to this blog as they are released.

articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways

Public Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) speed up deployment, but anyone can publish one, so they should never be trusted based on their name or description alone.

Malicious or misconfigured AMIs can carry vulnerable software, embedded malware, exposed credentials, or insecure configurations that compromise workloads as soon as they launch.

The whoAMI attack, disclosed by Datadog Security Labs, shows how attackers can publish look-alike images that get picked up by pipelines that don’t verify the AMI owner.

A single compromised source image can spread through Golden AMIs to every account, region, and workload built from it, and images that aren’t rebuilt regularly drift out of date.

Validating image owners, rebuilding Golden AMIs regularly, using AWS Allowed AMIs, and continuously monitoring with Qualys TotalCloud help keep malicious and misconfigured images out of production.

Introduction

A developer or CI/CD pipeline searches for an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) using a familiar image name. If the workflow does not verify the image’s owner, it may select a malicious image that resembles a trusted one. This is the risk highlighted by Datadog Security Labs’ whoAMI research: an image-selection mistake can introduce a supply chain compromise before an application even starts running.

The impact extends beyond image selection. Malicious or misconfigured AMIs can introduce vulnerable software, embedded malware, exposed credentials, or insecure configurations into newly launched EC2 instances. When such images are incorporated into Golden AMI workflows and reused across environments, the resulting risks can propagate to multiple workloads.

Securing AMIs therefore requires more than checking a few cloud configuration settings. Organizations need to validate image provenance, assess image contents before deployment, secure infrastructure automation, and monitor workloads for signs of compromise.

This article examines the risks associated with public and misconfigured AMIs, analyzes relevant attack scenarios, maps supported behaviors to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and explores how AWS security controls and Qualys capabilities can help reduce risk throughout the AMI lifecycle.

AMIs Provide the Foundation for EC2 Deployments

An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is a template used to launch Amazon EC2 instances. It includes the operating system, installed software, configuration, and storage mappings needed to create an instance.

AMIs can be private or public:

Private AMIs are shared with authorized AWS accounts and are commonly used to maintain standardized, organization-approved images.

Public AMIs are available to AWS customers in the region where they are shared. They allow organizations to reuse community- or vendor-provided images, reducing the effort required to prepare new EC2 instances.

Security Risks of Public AMIs

Using public AMIs introduces multiple security risks because organizations rely on third-party-maintained software and configurations.

The primary risks include:

Outdated operating systems and vulnerable software packages

Embedded malware or cryptominers

Hardcoded credentials or sensitive configuration files

Accidental publication of internal AMIs

Image impersonation through misleading names or descriptions

Supply chain compromise through insecure Golden AMIs

Although these risks differ in execution, they all originate from inadequate validation of image provenance and insufficient governance throughout the AMI lifecycle.

Attack Analysis

1. Malicious Public AMIs

Public AMIs published by unknown or untrusted users can intentionally contain malicious components designed to compromise workloads immediately after deployment.

Embedded Malware

Attackers may embed malware directly into an AMI before publishing it. Once an EC2 instance is launched, malicious payloads execute automatically, allowing attackers to establish persistence, communicate with command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, deploy ransomware, or mine cryptocurrency.

Vulnerable or Weaponized Software

Instead of embedding malware directly, attackers may intentionally distribute images containing outdated software with known vulnerabilities. Once deployed, these vulnerabilities can be exploited remotely to gain unauthorized access or to escalate privileges.

Image Impersonation (whoAMI Attack)

Datadog Security Labs disclosed the whoAMI attack, in which attackers publish malicious AMIs with names that closely resemble trusted vendor images.

If developers or automation pipelines search for AMIs by image name alone, without validating the image owner, a malicious image may be selected and deployed instead of the legitimate one.

This attack demonstrates that image metadata can serve as an effective attack vector even when the infrastructure code remains unchanged.

2. Misconfigured AMIs Can Introduce Inherited Security Weaknesses

An AMI need not be intentionally malicious to pose security risks. Images containing outdated software, exposed secrets, or insecure system settings can carry these weaknesses into newly launched EC2 instances.

Common examples include:

Unpatched operating systems and software packages

Hardcoded credentials or sensitive configuration files

Embedded SSH private keys

Insecure SSH authentication settings

Unnecessary services or insecure system configurations

These weaknesses can increase the attack surface of instances launched from the image. Depending on the configuration and surrounding security controls, they may expose workloads to unauthorized access, credential compromise, or exploitation of known vulnerabilities.

Security risks can also arise during deployment. For example, attaching an overly permissive IAM role to an EC2 instance can grant compromised workloads access to cloud resources beyond what they require. Similarly, accidentally sharing an internal AMI can expose an image to unauthorized parties.

3. Supply Chain Risks from Golden AMIs

Golden AMIs provide a standardized and secure baseline for enterprise deployments. However, if the source image is compromised, all derived images inherit the same vulnerabilities.

For example, if an organization creates a Golden AMI from:

an untrusted public AMI,

a vulnerable marketplace image, or

an internally compromised image,

Every EC2 instance launched from that Golden AMI inherits the same weaknesses.

This significantly amplifies the impact of a single compromised image by propagating vulnerabilities across multiple AWS accounts, regions, and production environments.

Version Drift

Even well-maintained Golden AMIs become outdated if they are not rebuilt regularly.

Organizations often patch running instances while continuing to deploy new workloads from older images. This creates inconsistent security baselines, leaving newly launched systems vulnerable to already-patched CVEs.

AMI Inventory and Lineage Challenges

Large enterprises frequently maintain hundreds of AMIs across multiple AWS accounts and Regions.

Without centralized inventory and lineage tracking, security teams struggle to determine:

which workloads originated from vulnerable images,

which Golden AMIs inherited vulnerabilities,

which production systems require immediate remediation.

Maintaining complete image lineage significantly improves incident response and vulnerability management.

MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

The following ATT&CK techniques represent behaviors that may occur across the AMI attack scenarios discussed in this article. Not every technique is necessarily present in every attack.

MITRE ATT&CK ID

Technique

Attack Description

T1608.001

Stage Capabilities: Upload Malware

Attackers upload backdoored AMIs to public repositories, including AWS Community AMIs, making malicious images available for unsuspecting users to download and deploy.

T1195

Supply Chain Compromise

Attackers introduce compromised system images into the infrastructure supply chain. When organizations incorporate these images into their Golden AMI workflows, malicious components can propagate to downstream workloads.

T1036.005

Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

Attackers use names that resemble trusted AMIs to mislead developers or automated image-selection workflows into selecting malicious images.

T1525

Implant Internal Image

Attackers implant malicious code into images within a victim’s cloud environment, potentially allowing malicious components to persist through subsequent deployments.

End-to-End Attack Scenario

A realistic attack chain may unfold as follows:

An attacker publishes a malicious public AMI using a trusted-looking name.

A developer or CI/CD pipeline searches for an image without validating the owner.

The malicious image is selected and used to create an internal Golden AMI.

The Golden AMI is replicated across multiple AWS accounts and Regions.

New EC2 instances inherit the malicious software or insecure configurations.

Malware establishes persistence and communicates with attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Attackers steal credentials, escalate privileges, move laterally, and compromise additional cloud resources.

Potential Impact

Deploying a malicious or misconfigured AMI can lead to:

Unauthorized access to EC2 instances

Credential theft

Data exfiltration

Cryptocurrency mining

Increased cloud costs

Lateral movement across AWS resources

Supply chain compromise

Regulatory and compliance violations

Reputational damage

Mitigation and Best Practices

Preventive Controls

Organizations should prevent vulnerable AMIs from entering production by implementing strong governance controls.

Recommended practices include:

Assess AMIs for vulnerabilities before deployment using services such as Amazon Inspector or Qualys TotalCloud AMI Scan.

Build and regularly rebuild Golden AMIs through CI/CD pipelines.

Automate Golden AMI creation and validation through CI/CD pipelines, incorporating the latest operating system patches, security updates, and hardened configurations before images are approved and distributed. Periodically rebuild and retire outdated images to prevent version drift, which can cause newly launched EC2 instances to inherit unpatched software, known vulnerabilities, or deprecated security configurations. This helps maintain consistent security baselines across deployments.

Validate image provenance by verifying publisher identity and AMI owner IDs.

Always define the AMI owner ID to prevent name confusion attacks.

AWS warning when omitting owners:

Restrict public sharing of internally created AMIs.

Avoid making AMIs public unless necessary and ensure all sensitive data is removed beforehand.

Use AWS Allowed AMIs to enforce trusted image sources.

Utilize AWS’s Allowed AMIs feature to enforce trust boundaries and restrict instance launches to vetted image sources.

Treat AMIs as third-party software dependencies that require security review before approval.

Detective Controls

Continuous monitoring is equally important.

Organizations should:

Monitor AWS CloudTrail for AMI creation, modification, sharing, and launch events.

Detect EC2 instances launched from unknown or unapproved AMIs.

Alert when AMIs become publicly accessible.

Monitor image usage across AWS accounts.

Enable drift detection for Golden AMIs.

Continuously scan deployed workloads for inherited vulnerabilities.

Governance and Lifecycle Management

Effective AMI governance extends beyond deployment.

Organizations should:

Maintain a centralized inventory of approved AMIs.

Track AMI lineage to understand parent-child image relationships.

Periodically review sharing permissions.

Remove obsolete or unused AMIs.

Integrate AMI validation into change management and deployment workflows.

Securing the AWS AMI Lifecycle with Qualys

Securing AMIs requires visibility and protection across multiple stages of the cloud deployment lifecycle. Organizations must assess images before deployment, identify infrastructure misconfigurations, monitor deployed workloads, and respond to potential threats.

Qualys provides capabilities across these stages through its TotalCloud CNAPP platform and complementary vulnerability management and endpoint security solutions.

1. Assess AMIs Before Deployment

Qualys TotalCloud provides an AMI Scan capability that uses snapshot-based scanning to assess Amazon Machine Images before deployment, without requiring an EC2 instance to be launched or an agent to be installed.

The assessment helps identify operating system vulnerabilities, missing patches, outdated software components, and configuration issues within AMIs.

Integrating AMI scanning into image-building and Golden AMI promotion workflows allows security teams to assess images before they are approved for production use. This helps reduce the likelihood of deploying images containing known security weaknesses.

However, vulnerability assessment alone does not establish the authenticity of an AMI publisher or guarantee that an image is free from malicious code. Organizations should continue to validate AMI ownership and publisher information using AWS-native controls.

2. Identify Infrastructure Misconfigurations Before Deployment

Qualys Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Security helps identify security misconfigurations in supported infrastructure templates before resources are deployed.

By integrating IaC scanning into CI/CD workflows, development and security teams can identify insecure infrastructure definitions in Terraform and AWS CloudFormation templates before they reach production.

This complements AMI scanning by assessing the infrastructure deployment process, helping organizations identify configuration weaknesses that could expose EC2 workloads.

3. Strengthen Cloud Posture and Workload Security

Qualys TotalCloud combines Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection (CWP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM) capabilities to provide visibility into cloud security risks.

These capabilities help organizations:

Assess vulnerabilities across supported cloud workloads and prioritize remediation based on risk.

Identify excessive cloud permissions and risky identity relationships that could increase the impact of a compromised workload.

This helps security teams understand not only the security state of an AMI, but also the configuration and identity risks associated with the EC2 instances launched from it.

4. Remediate Vulnerabilities and Automate Security Workflows

Identifying vulnerabilities is only one part of securing the AMI lifecycle. Organizations must also ensure that identified weaknesses are addressed across running workloads and future image builds.

Qualys Vulnerability Management, Detection and Response (VMDR) helps identify and prioritize vulnerabilities across supported assets. Qualys Patch Management can support deploying applicable security patches to supported running workloads.

Qualys Flow and TotalCloud workflow automation capabilities can further help operationalize security findings through customized remediation workflows, incident routing, and supported integrations.

For Golden AMI environments, organizations should incorporate remediation into their image-building pipelines and periodically rebuild approved images to ensure that future deployments inherit updated security baselines.

Extending Image Security Across Multi-Cloud Environments

Although this article focuses on AWS AMIs, similar risks exist across cloud platforms wherever organizations use reusable machine images to provision workloads. Azure and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), for example, provide image services that allow teams to create, share, and reuse standardized images across their environments.

The terminology and image-sharing mechanisms differ across providers, but the underlying security concerns remain similar: an image may contain outdated software, insecure configurations, or embedded sensitive information, while insufficient governance can expose internally maintained images or allow untrusted images to enter deployment workflows.

Across these platforms, organizations should maintain visibility into image metadata and apply consistent governance practices. This includes identifying image owners and sources, restricting access to approved images, reviewing sharing permissions, assessing image contents for vulnerabilities and exposed secrets, and periodically retiring outdated images.

For organizations operating in multi-cloud environments, centralized cloud security monitoring can help identify configuration weaknesses and exposure to vulnerabilities across image-related resources and the workloads launched from them. Treating machine images as part of the software supply chain, rather than simply as infrastructure artifacts, helps organizations apply consistent security governance from image creation through deployment and ongoing workload operation.

Conclusion

Public AMIs provide significant operational benefits, but they should never be trusted by default. As cloud-native deployments become increasingly automated, AMIs have become critical components of the software supply chain whose integrity directly affects the security of downstream workloads.

Securing the AMI lifecycle requires organizations to validate image sources, assess images for vulnerabilities before deployment, maintain governed Golden AMI workflows, and continuously monitor the workloads launched from them. AWS-native capabilities such as Allowed AMIs help restrict image usage to approved sources, while security solutions such as Qualys TotalCloud help identify image vulnerabilities, cloud misconfigurations, and risks across deployed workloads.

What is the whoAMI attack?

Attackers publish malicious AMIs with names that resemble trusted vendor images. Pipelines that search by name and do not verify the owner can select the malicious image.

No. Anyone can publish a public AMI. Trust comes from the owner ID and publisher, not the name or description.
